title: Project & setup
summary: Build, test, and understand the correctness-first CKKS GPU project.
text: ntt-gpu ¶ GPU-accelerated RNS NTT, key-switching, and automorphism kernels for FHE (and, by shared core operation, ZK proving). Target: best-in-class, honestly-benchmarked CUDA kernels. Status: Layer 1 (CPU ref backend) complete and cross-verified — 2026-10-29. Layer 2 written and Mac-proven (schedule simulator green); GPU gates light up automatically wherever nvcc exists. Roadmap ¶ v0.1 (2027-01-31): correct, tested RNS NTT CUDA kernel + benchmark table (RTX 4090 + RTX 5090), e.g. "2^16 coefficients, 40-bit limbs: X ms, N× vs OpenFHE CPU". Layer 1 — CPU reference negacyclic NTT + Python big-int oracle (2026-10-29) Layer 2 — CUDA kernel, validated on the same vectors 2a — the GPU stage schedule ( include/ntt/dev_core.hpp ), proven on CPU by a portable simulator gate ( device_schedule_check ) at n = 64 / 1024 / 4096 2b — the kernels themselves ( src/cuda/ntt_kernels.cu ), thin wrappers around the proven schedule; GPU gates register automatically under nvcc 2c — first run on a rented GPU (see below), bench table recorded 2d — systematic benchmark and autotuning matrix across GPU launch parameters and NTT implementations; select winners per ring size, RNS tower count, and latency/throughput objective v0.2 (2027-04-30): key-switching / automorphism kernels; first upstream PRs. Benchmarking and tuning are part of the implementation, not a final reporting step. The primary target is RTX 5090 ( sm_120 ), with RTX 4090 ( sm_89 ) as the cross-architecture control. The matrix includes N = 4096..65536 , realistic CKKS modulus widths and tower counts, threads/block, values/thread, radix, register and shared-memory use, split/tile shape, batch size, streams, twiddle representation, and transfer policy. It compares the correctness baseline, optimized two-pass variants, radix-4/8 register staging, and a coalesced Four-Step/transpose path. Kernel-only and end-to-end results are reported separately. See docs/benchmark-tuning-plan.md . Build & test ¶ No dependencies beyond CMake, a C++20 compiler, and Python 3 (stdlib only). Without a CUDA toolkit (e.g. the dev Mac): cmake -S . -B build && cmake --build build -j && ctest --test-dir build --output-on-failure Six gates: vector generation ×3 sizes (RNS primes + 2N-th roots of unity at n = 64/1024/4096), unit tests (modular arithmetic, bit-reversal, forward/inverse roundtrip, NTT-multiply vs O(N²) schoolbook mod x^N+1), the cross-language oracle check — the C++ fast transform must equal a definitional naive O(N²) big-integer transform in Python, limb by limb, with position-wise CRT reconstruction over all limbs — and the device-schedule check: the simulator ( src/device_sim.cpp ) runs the exact stage bodies the CUDA kernels run and must match the CPU reference array-for-array, bit-reversed order included. For a ready-to-run macOS VS Code setup, including an N=8 example and LLDB single-stepping instructions, see docs/vscode-debugging.md . With nvcc present, CMake auto-detects it and adds ntt_cuda_cli plus three GPU gates, unchanged commands otherwise: cuda_oracle_crosscheck (the same Python oracle against the CUDA binary — its output is byte-identical to ntt_cli ), cuda_matches_ref (byte-compare of both binaries' transform output at n = 1024 and 4096; valid at any size, use a 2^18 fixture freely), and cuda_verify (in-process GPU-vs-ref forward/roundtrip/multiply on the fixtures plus a generated n = 65536 case). Exact OpenFHE compatibility ¶ The OpenFHE gate pins OpenFHE 1.6.1 at commit b59e1f291965f14fbee5172cd83a20f5b856204f , builds it under the ignored build/ tree, and compares the public NativePoly coefficient/evaluation conversion against NegacyclicNtt element for element: bash scripts/openfhe_setup.sh openfhe_exact_compat covers N = 4096, 8192, 16384, 32768, 65536 , two OpenFHE-selected CKKS-sized modulus widths (50 and 59 bits), zero, maximum, ramp, and deterministic-random coefficient inputs, plus independent random evaluation-domain inputs for inverse transforms. Equality includes OpenFHE's exact bit-reversed evaluation ordering; this is not a decrypt-tolerance test. The CUDA gates already require GPU output to equal the same CPU reference, so the two exact gates compose to OpenFHE == reference == CUDA on GPU hardware. The ordinary dependency-free build remains unchanged. To reuse an existing OpenFHE installation instead of the setup script, configure with -DNTT_ENABLE_OPENFHE_COMPAT=ON and point CMAKE_PREFIX_PATH at its install prefix; CMake requires version 1.6.1 exactly. Architecture default: sm_89 + sm_120 when the toolkit is ≥ 12.8, else sm_89 (the build embeds compute_89 PTX, which a 5090 driver JITs) — one build runs on both rentable cards. Override with -DCMAKE_CUDA_ARCHITECTURES=native (CMake ≥ 3.24) on a single known box. First session on a rented GPU ¶ bash scripts/autodl_setup.sh # or: NTT_REPO_DIR=... NTT_CUDA_ARCH=... Idempotent one-shot: finds nvcc (PATH or /usr/local/cuda/bin ), clone-or-pull, configure + build, run every gate, run the bench sweep, and write VERDICT.txt (GPU name, driver, toolkit, arch sanity check, per-gate results, bench table). Exit code reflects the gates. Bench numbers are attached to that hardware header or they don't get quoted. Design ¶ Two backends behind one interface: ref — CPU reference (correctness is defined here; big-int-checked test vectors) cuda — GPU kernel (validated against ref on identical vectors) The CUDA port's index math lives once in include/ntt/dev_core.hpp , compiled by the Mac simulator and by the kernels alike, so schedule and device cannot drift; the reference arithmetic ( mod_arith.hpp ) is __host__ __device__ , so the GPU runs literally the reference mul_mod . The schedule is a two-pass split at 256: pass 1 over 256 strided groups (the far stages, whose pair distance is a multiple of 256, pair values sharing their offset mod 256), pass 2 over contiguous 256-tiles (the near stages). All 16 stages at N = 65,536 run on shared-memory counters; the "mix" between passes is pure data movement (scatter strided, gather contiguous), so VRAM traffic is 4 round-trips per value instead of the 14 a global-memory phase would cost — and one forward is 2 kernel launches. v1 uses the __uint128_t division lowering on device — emulated there, and honestly slow; the bench table quantifies exactly that pre-Barrett gap, and Barrett/Montgomery lands later behind the same signature with a dedicated cross-check. The simulator is serial by nature: it proves the math, not barriers or launch configs — the GPU gates exist for that residue. Benchmarks are only ever reported from the cuda backend on named hardware. Transform convention (see include/ntt/ntt.hpp ): ψ a primitive 2N-th root of unity mod q, forward: A_j = Σ_i a_i·ψ^((2j+1)·i) mod q — evaluation at the odd powers of ψ, where x^N+1 splits into linear factors. Docs ¶ The documentation now builds as one HTML engineering notebook: shared navigation, search, learning pages, research, plans, and a daily journal recording outcomes, reasoning, evidence, open questions, and next steps. python3 -m venv .venv .venv/bin/python -m pip install -r docs/requirements.txt .venv/bin/python scripts/build_docs.py --check python3 -m http.server 8000 --bind 127.0.0.1 --directory build/docs-site Open http://127.0.0.1:8000/ . Markdown remains editable source; the generated site publishes HTML. The existing interactive explainers also work independently. See writing and publishing for GitHub Pages setup and the daily-entry workflow. These optional dependencies do not affect the C++ build. docs/butterfly-explained.html — an interactive, dependency-free beginner's explainer: why the NTT is built from butterfly units, from the one-line definition through the negacyclic fold rule to the full N=8 network (open in any browser). docs/gpu-ntt-explained.html — the GPU port explained from zero: the machine's concepts and real parameters (threads, blocks, SMs, the 4090/5090 numbers), then how this repo splits the NTT into strided groups and contiguous tiles so every stage runs on a shared-memory counter. docs/gpu-ntt-survey.md — primary-source survey of GPU NTT and CKKS implementations, with the techniques this project can absorb. docs/gpu-selection-survey.md — primary-source comparison of RTX 5090, RTX 4090, RTX PRO 6000, L40S, A100, H100/H200, and B200 for this project's exact u32 / u64 modular-arithmetic workload. docs/benchmark-tuning-plan.md — reproducible benchmark matrix and tuning/selection rules for GPU parameters and kernel variants. docs/openfhe-integration-plan.md — the tracked 95-day implementation plan (plus risk reserve) from the current NTT baseline through GPU base conversion, Hybrid key switching, and validated OpenFHE integration. docs/vscode-debugging.md — shared VS Code build, run, test, and LLDB step-debugging setup for the small CPU NTT example. Provenance ¶ Independent clean-room implementation. Contains no code, data, or artifacts from any past or present employer. Development history is fully documented in this repository's git log from the first commit. License ¶ TBD (decide before accepting outside contributions).

title: NTT & butterflies
summary: From the direct NTT sum to butterflies, twiddles, and the negacyclic transform.
text: ntt-gpu · a beginner's field guide How an NTT really works. An NTT turns one expensive polynomial multiplication into many small, repeated butterfly operations. no prerequisites examples use mod 5 and mod 17 interactive diagrams × w a b a + w·b a − w·b the only shape this whole page needs The idea in four steps Read this first. The chapters below explain why each step is valid. 1 · START A polynomial is stored as a list of coefficients. 2 · TRANSFORM The NTT evaluates that list at special modular points. 3 · REUSE A butterfly computes one shared sum-and-difference pair. 4 · REPEAT N/2 butterflies across log₂N stages finish the transform. Shortest path: data → NTT → sum to butterfly → butterfly → network → negacyclic . The other chapters are optional detail. Contents 01 Input: coefficients 02 Special points 03 What the NTT does 04 Why direct is slow 05 Sum → butterflies 06 One butterfly 07 Full N = 8 network 08 Work saved 09 Negacyclic NTT 10 Code mapping 01 Start with coefficients The input is a list of N numbers . In this page, that list represents a polynomial: 3 slot 0 7 slot 1 1 slot 2 9 slot 3 4 slot 4 0 slot 5 5 slot 6 2 slot 7 For this project, N ranges from 4,096 to 65,536. We need to multiply two such lists efficiently: multiply two lists of length N, get back a list of length N The NTT (Number Theoretic Transform) is how that multiplication gets done fast. (How the product stays length N — the fold rule — is chapter 9's story.) 02 Choose special modular points Modulo 17, start at 1 and keep multiplying by 2. After eight different values, the sequence returns to 1: The wheel — the eight powers of 2, mod 17 · start at 1, keep multiplying by 2 1 2 4 8 16 15 13 9 ω⁰ ω¹ ω² ω³ ω⁴ = −1 ω⁵ ω⁶ ω⁷ dashed diameters: opposite points sum to 17 = q — each is the other's negative (property iii, halfway = minus) Eight different numbers, then the ninth step lands back on 1. The powers of 2 form a closed loop of exactly 8 points — a wheel . Such a number is a root of unity ("unity" just means 1): \(ω^N = 1\) , and primitive if no earlier power comes home. Everything the NTT relies on is a property of this wheel: Nothing sacred about 2 — mod 17 offers four primitive 8th roots: 2, 8, 9, 15. Each walks the same eight points in a different order; 2 just gives the easiest multiplication table. Optional: why these points make the NTT fast i. Closed: multiply = move Powers never leave the wheel: \(ω^{a}\,ω^{b} = ω^{a+b}\) — multiplying just adds positions, a clock for multiplication (the logarithm trick). Why: one number generates all N plug-in points, one multiplication each. ii. Distinct: nothing is lost A primitive root visits N different points, so N plugged-in values pin the list down exactly — the coordinates are reversible. Why: the transform has an inverse. The one demand on the prime: N | q−1 ( ntt.hpp:61 ). iii. Halfway = minus \(ω^{N/2} = -1\) : opposite points are negatives (above: 1↔16, 2↔15, 4↔13, 8↔9 — each pair sums to 17). Why: the ± that makes output pairs — the butterfly's two wings (chapter 6). iv. Squaring = a half wheel Every second point closes after N/2 steps: a half-size wheel with root ω². Why: wheels nest — the transform builds itself from half-size copies, the source of every "repeat" in chapter 5. Why not just any N distinct numbers? Any N distinct points make chapter 3's trick correct . Only wheel points make it fast : the shared brackets of chapter 5 are this wheel's symmetries showing up as algebra. The speed of the NTT is wheel symmetry. 03 What the NTT does A list like \((2, 1)\) is a tiny machine: plug a number t in for x, get a value out. And plugged-in values multiply one by one: \[(A\cdot B)(t) = A(t)\times B(t)\] One multiplication, no crossing terms — and it holds for every t. Both roads below use \(t = 2\) (mod 5); change any coefficient and they still agree: Interactive · two roads, one answer (mod 5) A slot 0 − 2 + A slot 1 · x − 1 + B slot 0 − 3 + B slot 1 · x − 2 + ROAD 1 · EXPAND BY HAND ROAD 2 · PLUG IN t = 2 ✓ the two roads agree Road 1 costs four multiplies and still knows the product at only one point. Road 2 costs one multiply — and the equation below runs Road 2 at every wheel point at once. To pin the product down we need its values at N different points — chapter 2's wheel supplies them. the definition · the whole transform in one line \[A_j = a_0+a_1\omega^j+a_2\omega^{2j}+a_3\omega^{3j}+\cdots \pmod{q}\] Evaluating the list at all N wheel points is the NTT . Output j is the list plugged in at wheel point ωʲ — and because the points are distinct (wheel property ii), the transform inverts: evaluate → multiply pointwise → invert replaces a list multiplication with N plain multiplies. The rest of this page makes that round trip cheap. Why "NTT" and not "FFT"? The FFT does this with decimals — but decimals round, and rounding errors compound. The NTT does the same idea with whole numbers mod a prime : exact forever. Its wheels exist whenever N | q−1 — checked at ntt.hpp:61 . 04 Direct evaluation is too expensive The equation demands N outputs, each a sum of N products — computed one by one, that's \(N \times N\) multiplications per transform: Interactive · feel the N² pain list length N = 1024 2 8 … 2 18 At N = 65,536: 4.3 billion products per transform — and transforms run constantly. The escape plan: find the repeats hiding inside the equation. 05 Turn the NTT sum into butterflies Start from the ordinary NTT definition. For output index k, direct evaluation forms one N-term sum: \[ A_k = \sum_{r=0}^{N-1} a_r\,\omega^{rk}, \qquad 0\leq k<N \] The optimization is not an approximation. Split that exact sum by whether the input index r is even or odd. Write \(r = 2m\) for even indices and \(r = 2m+1\) for odd indices: \[ \begin{aligned} \textcolor{#14655A}{E_k} &= \sum_{m=0}^{N/2-1} a_{2m}\,(\omega^2)^{mk} \\ \textcolor{#C2410C}{O_k} &= \sum_{m=0}^{N/2-1} a_{2m+1}\,(\omega^2)^{mk} \\[0.5em] A_k &= \textcolor{#14655A}{E_k} + \omega^k\,\textcolor{#C2410C}{O_k} \end{aligned} \] Now look at the output halfway around the wheel. Since \(ω^{N/2} = -1\) , its odd half changes sign while its even half does not: \[ \begin{aligned} A_{k+N/2} &= \textcolor{#14655A}{E_k} - \omega^k\,\textcolor{#C2410C}{O_k} \\ t &= \omega^k O_k \\[0.5em] (A_k,\ A_{k+N/2}) &= (E_k+t,\ E_k-t) \end{aligned} \] That final pair is one butterfly. The two outputs reuse the same \(E[k]\) , the same \(O[k]\) , and—most importantly—the same multiplication \(t = ω^k\,O[k]\) . 1 · DIRECT Compute N independent sums, each with N terms. \(\text{cost: } O(N^2)\) 2 · SPLIT Separate every sum into its even-index and odd-index terms. \(A=E+\omega^k O\) 3 · SHARE Pair outputs k and k+N/2. They share everything except a sign. \(E+t,\ E-t\) 4 · RECURSE E and O are smaller NTTs using the root ω². Split them again. \(\log_2 N\text{ stages}\) Why the optimization keeps working \(ω^{2}\) is an N/2-th root of unity, so E and O have exactly the same shape as the original problem, only half as large. Repeating the split reaches two-value problems. Each level contains N/2 butterflies, and there are log₂N levels. The N = 4 example below expands the same identity completely. Take \(a = (a_{0}, a_{1}, a_{2}, a_{3})\) and write all four outputs longhand. (Here \(ω^{4} = 1\) , so exponents wrap: ω⁶ = ω², ω⁹ = ω.) Worked example: show the N = 4 algebra \[ \begin{aligned} A_0 &= a_0+a_1+a_2+a_3 \\ A_1 &= a_0+a_1\omega+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega^3 \\ A_2 &= a_0+a_1\omega^2+a_2+a_3\omega^2 \\ A_3 &= a_0+a_1\omega^3+a_2\omega^2+a_3\omega \end{aligned} \] Four outputs × four terms — sixteen products if you charge ahead blindly. Now regroup every line, even-position terms first, odd-position terms second, and stare at what repeats: \[ \begin{aligned} A_0 &= \textcolor{#14655A}{(a_0+a_2)}+\textcolor{#C2410C}{(a_1+a_3)} \\ A_2 &= \textcolor{#14655A}{(a_0+a_2)}-\textcolor{#C2410C}{(a_1+a_3)} \\[0.5em] A_1 &= \textcolor{#14655A}{(a_0+a_2\omega^2)}+\omega\,\textcolor{#C2410C}{(a_1+a_3\omega^2)} \\ A_3 &= \textcolor{#14655A}{(a_0+a_2\omega^2)}-\omega\,\textcolor{#C2410C}{(a_1+a_3\omega^2)} \end{aligned} \] The same two brackets sit inside both outputs of each pair — and the multiply \(ω\,(a_{1}+a_{3}ω^{2})\) is shared too. One more squeeze: halfway around the wheel is minus (property iii), \(ω^{2} = -1\) , so \((a_{0}+a_{2}ω^{2}) = a_{0}-a_{2}\) and \((a_{1}+a_{3}ω^{2}) = a_{1}-a_{3}\) . Extract the four inner results: \[ \begin{aligned} p &= a_0+a_2, & q &= a_0-a_2 \\ r &= a_1+a_3, & s &= a_1-a_3 \end{aligned} \qquad (w=1) \] The brackets are already butterflies — each line is one unit fed with two raw coefficients. The final assembly is two more: \[ \begin{aligned} A_0 &= p+r, & A_2 &= p-r && (w=1) \\ A_1 &= q+\omega s, & A_3 &= q-\omega s && (w=\omega) \end{aligned} \] Count: 2 + 2 = 4 butterflies — \((N/2)\,\log_{2}N\) for N = 4, and exactly stages 1–2 of chapter 7's picture. Level 1 feeds level 2, and the four outputs fall out. For general N, name the halves the way the books do — E for the evens-machine, O for the odds-machine — and every pair of slots (j and its opposite j + N/2) is assembled from them: \[ \begin{aligned} \mathrm{out}[j] &= E+wO \\ \mathrm{out}[j+N/2] &= E-wO \end{aligned} \] Where does that minus come from? Wheel property iii Halfway around, every point is the negative of its mirror: \(ω^{j+N/2} = -ω^{j}\) (mod 17, ω = 4: ω² = 16 = −1). The repo checks this exact fact at ntt.hpp:66 : psi^n == q−1 . The same derivation with real numbers — set the coefficients yourself: Interactive · both levels, real numbers — mod 17, ω = 4 (ω² = 16 ≡ −1) a₀ − 3 + a₁ · x − 1 + a₂ · x² − 5 + a₃ · x³ − 2 + Change any coefficient: level 1 feeds level 2, four butterflies total — and the answer never dares to disagree with the one-line definition. One multiply, one add, one subtract; two values in, two out. That is the fast algorithm's only moving part. At N = 8 it simply nests one level deeper — chapter 7's machine, where we go next. 06 Meet the butterfly You met this unit four times in chapter 5. Draw its formulas as a circuit: two wires in, two out, crossing once — from the side, two wings. Someone in 1969 said "butterfly" , and the name never left. It comes in two costumes — same wings, the multipliers ride different legs: × w + − a b a + b·w a − b·w 1 2 DIT — ① multiply the input , ② add / subtract · what chapters 5–7 derive + − × w a b a + b (a − b)·w 1 2 DIF — ① add / subtract, ② multiply the difference output · the same unit, run the other way Same two wings — only the order of multiply vs ± differs (the gold ①②). DIT multiplies before the crossing, DIF after it. (The repo's negacyclic forward adds one refinement on top of DIF — a ladder constant ψ^d on the input leg; that is chapter 10's loop.) 07 Connect butterflies into stages Eight wires, values flowing left to right; every X is one butterfly. Press play (arithmetic mod 17, ω = 2), or click any butterfly to inspect it. The partner distance doubles each stage — 1, 2, 4 — the recursion of chapter 5, unrolled one level more and laid out flat. Interactive · the N = 8 butterfly network (mod 17) ▶ play all stages next stage ⏭ reset stage 0 / 3 — values not yet transformed Hover or click a butterfly (the X crossings) to see exactly what it computes. wire (a value flowing right) butterfly value chip (appears as stages complete) Why are the inputs scrambled? The leftmost values are in bit-reversed order (0,4,2,6,1,5,3,7 — index in binary, read backwards). That one upfront shuffle lets every stage read its partners from nearby positions and the outputs arrive in natural order. The repo ships the mirror image: a DIF forward (natural inputs, bit-reversed outputs ) paired with a DIT inverse that consumes exactly that order — so in the real pipeline the two permutations cancel and no bit-reversal pass exists at all ( bitrev.hpp documents the permutation itself). And the negacyclic variant? This network is the plain ("cyclic") transform. The negacyclic variant — chapter 10 — is the same network with its stage twiddles scaled by wheel powers: same butterflies, one pass ( ntt.hpp:87 ). 08 How much work is saved? Count the X's in the picture: 4 per stage × 3 stages = 12 butterflies for N = 8, against the 64 products of computing chapter 3's equation output-by-output. In general: \((N/2) \, \log_{2}(N)\) butterflies versus \(N^{2}\) products. The two complexities, side by side: Interactive · direct N² vs butterflies (N/2)·log₂N — log–log plot direct — each output on its own (N² products) butterflies — shared brackets ((N/2)·log₂N units) hover the plot — at N = 65,536 the direct line stands 8,192× above the butterfly line On the log–log plot both curves are straight lines — but with different slopes: every doubling of N doubles the butterfly count and quadruples the direct count, so the gap itself doubles at every step. (And the direct tally counts only multiplications; a butterfly's add and subtract are cheaper still.) 09 CKKS uses the negacyclic form One loose end from chapter 1: the operation there was "multiply two lists, get back a list of the same length N ." But plain multiplication lengthens the list: \[(2+x)(3+2x)=6+7x+2x^2\] If every multiplication grew the list, nothing could chain. The fix is one fold rule, in exactly two flavors: \[ \begin{aligned} x^N &= +1 && \text{cyclic: wrap with a plus} \\ x^N &= -1 && \text{negacyclic: wrap with a minus} \end{aligned} \] The cyclic fold is precisely the world of chapters 3–7: every ω-wheel point satisfies x^N = ω^N = 1. The negacyclic fold is the one this repo implements. With \(x^{2} = -1\) (N = 2, mod 5), the overflow folds back like this: \[ 6+7x+2x^2 \;\longmapsto\; (6-2)+7x \;\equiv\; 4+2x \pmod{5} \] All numbers live mod some prime (here mod 5) — only the remainder after dividing survives, so numbers stay tiny forever. Which points respect the minus fold? Those with \(x^N = -1\) — the roots of \(x^N + 1\) . They are the odd steps of a doubled wheel: a number ψ with \(ψ^N = -1\) closes after 2N points, and \((ψ^{\mathrm{odd}})^N = (-1)^{\mathrm{odd}} = -1\) . Mod 17, ψ = 6, and \(ψ^{2} = ω\) — its even steps are chapter 2's wheel: The doubled wheel · ψ = 6, a 16-th root of unity mod 17 (ψ⁸ = −1, ψ² = ω) even steps = the ω wheel: 1 ψ⁰ 2 ψ² 4 ψ⁴ 8 ψ⁶ 16 ψ⁸ 15 ψ¹⁰ 13 ψ¹² 9 ψ¹⁴ odd steps = negacyclic: 6 ψ¹ 12 ψ³ 7 ψ⁵ 14 ψ⁷ 11 ψ⁹ 5 ψ¹¹ 10 ψ¹³ 3 ψ¹⁵ spot-check one highlighted point: 6⁸ = (6²)⁴ = 2⁴ = 16 ≡ −1 (mod 17) ✓ · chapter 3's t = 2 mod 5 was exactly an odd step of the small doubled wheel there (2² ≡ −1, 2⁴ ≡ 1) The key substitution: pre-twist, then use the ordinary NTT Let \(ω = ψ^{2}\) and pre-twist coefficient r as \(b[r] = a[r]\,ψ^r\) . An ordinary cyclic NTT of b then gives \(\sum_{r=0}^{N-1} b_r\omega^{rk} = \sum_{r=0}^{N-1} a_r\psi^{(2k+1)r}\) . In other words, the twist moves evaluation from the even powers of ψ to exactly the odd powers—the roots of x^N+1. The inverse runs the cyclic inverse and multiplies coefficient r by \(ψ^{-r}\) . What stays the same The radix-2 network, paired indices, number of stages, and N/2 butterflies per stage do not change. \[ \begin{aligned} u' &= u+v \\ v' &= (u-v)\,w \end{aligned} \] What negacyclic changes The ψ twist changes the factors carried by the butterfly. This repo folds it into the same pass instead of storing a separate twist table. \[ \begin{aligned} u' &= u+cv \\ v' &= (u-cv)\,w \end{aligned} \] For the repo's forward DIF loop, a stage pairs entries distance \(d\) apart. Its folded factors are: \[ \begin{aligned} c_d &= \psi^d \\ w_{d,j} &= \psi^{\frac{N}{d}j} = \omega^{\frac{N}{2d}j} \\[0.5em] \mathrm{upper}' &= \mathrm{upper}+c_d\,\mathrm{lower} \\ \mathrm{lower}' &= (\mathrm{upper}-c_d\,\mathrm{lower})\,w_{d,j} \end{aligned} \] The group number does not select the twiddle . At a fixed stage, every group repeats the same sequence: j starts at 0, so \(w = 1\) , then advances by \(ψ^{N/d}\) for each butterfly offset. Negacyclic therefore changes the factors, not the network's pairing pattern. The inverse uses reciprocal ψ factors, reverses the stage direction, and applies the final \(N^{-1}\) scale. 10 Map the picture to code Here is the actual loop from this repo's CPU reference ( include/ntt/ntt.hpp , the forward DIF sweep — twist folded in as ladder constants, natural values in, bit-reversed values out). Read the comments with chapter 7 open next to it — every line is a part of the picture: for ( uint64_t stage_pair_distance = n_ / 2 ; stage_pair_distance >= 1 ; stage_pair_distance >>= 1 ) { const uint64_t ladder_twiddle = pow_mod (psi_, stage_pair_distance, q_); // c_d = ψ^d const uint64_t twiddle_step = pow_mod (psi_, n_ / stage_pair_distance, q_); // ψ^(N/d) for ( uint64_t group_start_index = 0 ; group_start_index < n_; group_start_index += 2 * stage_pair_distance) { uint64_t twiddle_power = 1 ; // j = 0 for ( uint64_t pair_offset = 0 ; pair_offset < stage_pair_distance; ++pair_offset) { const uint64_t upper_index = group_start_index + pair_offset; const uint64_t lower_index = upper_index + stage_pair_distance; const uint64_t upper_value = values[upper_index]; const uint64_t scaled_lower_value = mul_mod (ladder_twiddle, values[lower_index], q_); values[upper_index] = add_mod (upper_value, scaled_lower_value, q_); // upper + c_d·lower values[lower_index] = mul_mod ( sub_mod (upper_value, scaled_lower_value, q_), twiddle_power, q_); // (upper − c_d·lower)·w_d,j twiddle_power = mul_mod (twiddle_power, twiddle_step, q_); } } } Three nested loops, one idea: for every butterfly in every stage — u+v, u−v. The CUDA port ahead just assigns each X to one GPU thread and each stage to one kernel launch. The picture is the architecture. The whole page in one breath A root of unity generates a wheel of N exact plug-in points that multiply like clock positions; the NTT is its one-line equation — the list evaluated at every wheel point. Computing that directly costs N² products; expanded longhand, the outputs share brackets, and each shared pair costs one multiply, one add, one subtract — a butterfly. Tiled across log₂N stages, N² collapses to (N/2)·log₂N: at N = 65,536, from 4.3 billion products down to 524,288 butterflies. The negacyclic variant plugs in at the odd steps of a doubled wheel (ψ^N = −1) to multiply under a fold-with-minus rule — the same butterflies inside. ntt-gpu · docs/butterfly-explained.html mod-5 & mod-17 examples · local KaTeX · view source freely Nov 2026

title: From CPU to CUDA
summary: Threads, blocks, shared memory, and this repository's two-pass GPU schedule.
text: ntt-gpu · a beginner's field guide to the GPU port How the NTT runs on a GPU. Each GPU thread handles a butterfly pair. Blocks keep small tiles in shared memory so several stages run without repeated VRAM traffic. target: RTX 5090 ring dimension: 4,096–65,536 256 threads per block every cook, same step, own ingredient The GPU plan in four steps This is the whole design. The chapters below explain the hardware and show the current code. 1 · SPLIT Give each independent butterfly pair to a GPU thread. 2 · LOAD A block gathers one 256-value group into shared memory. 3 · COMPUTE Run several stages locally, with a barrier between stages. 4 · REGROUP Use a far-pair pass and a near-pair pass to cover the full NTT. Current status: correctness-first baseline. Results must match the OpenFHE-compatible CPU reference exactly. The strided pass is not yet coalesced, so “four logical movements” does not mean four efficient VRAM transactions. Contents 01 CPU vs GPU 02 GPU vocabulary 03 Parallel butterflies 04 Two-pass design 05 Shared-memory tile 06 Code mapping 07 Synchronization 08 Memory cost 09 Current limits 01 CPU and GPU favor different work A CPU is good at a few complicated tasks. A GPU is good at many copies of the same small task. i. The CPU: a few master chefs Four to eight highly skilled cooks. Each one can do anything: chop, taste, adjust, change the plan mid-dish. Give one chef the whole recipe and they finish it alone — one dish at a time, but any dish. ii. The GPU: a brigade of line cooks Sixteen thousand cooks, but each one simple. The strict rule: at any moment, every cook performs the same step of the recipe — on their own portion of ingredients. Want 5000 cooks all whisking? Blazing. Want one cook to quietly deviate and taste-adjust? Nearly impossible. This model is called SIMT : many threads run the same instructions on different data. An NTT stage fits because every thread can apply the same butterfly formula to a different pair. The NTT is that work, almost embarrassingly so. One butterfly: u + c·v and (u − c·v)·w , over and over, billions of times. One recipe step, ten thousand portions. 02 Six GPU terms Six words run all GPU programming. None is deeper than "row", "shelf", and "roll call" — and the last column shows what each one is in this repo . Word Plain meaning In this repo thread One cook. Simple, follows the shared recipe, owns one portion of data at a time. we use T = 256 per block block A kitchen station: a fixed team of cooks who share a counter (see shared memory) and can synchronize with each other — and only with each other. one block owns one tile grid All stations laid out. Blocks live in a 2-D grid with an x and a y address — a built-in pair of numbers each block can read to know "which job am I". x = tile index, y = RNS limb shared memory The station's counter: small, fast, and private to one block. This is where the group lives while its stages run. 256 values = 2 KB per limb global memory The central warehouse (VRAM): huge (24 GB on a 4090), slow, shared by everyone. Data starts and ends here. the whole polynomial, all limbs kernel A function you write once that every thread of a launch runs — same code, each thread on its own slice. The word for "recipe" in GPU-speak. six kernels in ntt_kernels.cu A barrier ( __syncthreads() in code) is the station's roll call: every cook in the block must arrive before anyone leaves. Chapter 7 is about the one way to misuse it. how the pieces nest · one picture HOST your Mac / the CLI starts the kernel launch GPU — one chip GLOBAL MEMORY (VRAM) — the warehouse · shared by every block BLOCK (x=0, y=1) its counter (shared) BLOCK (x=1, y=1) its counter (shared) BLOCK (x=2, y=1) its counter (shared) every block loads its tile from VRAM, computes on its counter, writes back — blocks never see each other's counters thread (a cook) → inside a block (a station, with its private counter) → blocks tile the grid (x = tile, y = limb) → all inside one GPU around one warehouse Optional: RTX 4090 and RTX 5090 capacity estimates the picture, counted · for both rentable cards RTX 4090 RTX 5090 station groups (SMs) 128 170 cooks in flight (resident threads) 196,608 261,120 our 256-cook stations, resident at once 768 1,020 max cooks per block / per station 1,024 / 1,536 1,024 / 1,536 counter (shared) per block · per station 48 KB · ~100 KB 48 KB · ~100 KB warehouse (VRAM) 24 GB GDDR6X 32 GB GDDR7 pipe into the chip — VRAM bandwidth ≈ 1.0 TB/s ≈ 1.8 TB/s traffic inside the chip — shared, aggregate ≈ 40 TB/s ≈ 50 TB/s The design fact hiding in the last two rows: on-chip traffic is 40–50× the pipe into the chip — the entire reason the communication ladder (chapter 5) exists. Aggregate shared figures are order-of-magnitude estimates (per-SM path × SMs × boost clock); the ratio is the point, not the decimals. // the first rows are one multiplication chain — the table explains itself: 4090: 128 SMs × 1,536 threads/SM = 196,608 in flight ÷ 256 (our T) = 768 of our blocks resident 5090: 170 SMs × 1,536 = 261,120 ÷ 256 = 1,020 Why 256 and not the max 1,024 per block: smaller teams = six independent stations per island instead of one — each with its own counter, its own faster roll call, and a scheduler free to mix them. Grids bigger than resident (2,560 blocks at 40 limbs) simply queue for freed seats: the "waves". At N = 65,536 with 3 limbs, each pass launches 256 × 3 = 768 blocks . How many stay resident at once depends on threads, registers, shared memory, and the device's block limits; measure it instead of assuming one wave. 03 One stage has independent pairs Recall the NTT's shape: at every stage, the list is chopped into pairs, and each pair goes through one butterfly. At N = 8, one stage = four pairs. Click a stage and watch who pairs with whom: one stage at N = 8 · click a stage stage d = 4 stage d = 2 stage d = 1 pick 0,2,4,6 → 2 stages Every element belongs to exactly one pair per stage — the four butterflies share nothing . Four cooks, zero talking, any order. The fourth button is pass 1 of the real port in miniature (chapter 4). That "share nothing" is the entire secret. Because the pairs are disjoint , the four butterflies of a stage can run simultaneously, interleaved, in any order, on any cook — the final list is identical every time . A GPU stage is just: hand each pair to a cook, let them all fly at once, wait for the slowest, next stage. Disjointness also buys locality : a stage with distance d only ever pairs values inside one 2d-wide group, so a group of 2 k values owns its k smallest stages outright — the fact chapter 4 turns into the two-pass split, taken once with strided groups and once with contiguous tiles. Hold onto that sentence — it is also why a plain CPU simulator, running the same stage bodies serially, can prove the whole schedule before any GPU is rented. 04 Split the NTT into two passes So why not one giant block that does the whole transform? Size — a block's counter is capped at 48 KB, and the data is far bigger: where "1.5 MB" comes from · why the data can't sit on one counter 1 value (one coefficient, one limb) = 64 bits = 8 bytes one limb = 2¹⁶ values × 8 bytes = 524,288 B = 512 KB this repo = 3 limbs × 512 KB = 1,536 KB ≈ 1.5 MB real FHE = ~40 limbs × 512 KB ≈ 20 MB = 427× a block's whole 48 KB counter More limbs ≠ harder: each limb is one independent column of the grid (the y address) doing the identical dance — real coefficients are thousands of bits, kept as ~40 machine-word residues, one transform each. So how should a GPU run this? Walk the same road the port had to walk — four steps, each one forced by the step before: ① How the CPU does it — and where it hurts The reference ( ntt.hpp ) is one cook walking the list in order: stage by stage, pair by pair. At N = 8 that's four butterflies, one after another — even though chapter 3 proved they're independent. The picture below is the whole problem in miniature: same four butterflies, four units of wall time versus one . Fine at lecture size — but a real forward is 32,768 × 16 ≈ 524,288 butterflies per limb , ~21 million across 40 limbs. One cook at a few GHz drowns; that's the wall. ② First GPU idea: every pair on a cook, everything from VRAM Hand each pair of each stage to its own cook, all cooks at once, everyone reading and writing the warehouse directly. This works — and it is what a naive port does for every stage. But now count truck trips: every stage fetches its partners from VRAM and writes them back — one round-trip per stage per value, and there are 16 stages. The cooks spend their day at the loading dock (chapter 8's ladder: warehouse ≈ ×400 the counter). Arithmetic nearly free, delivery-bound anyway. ③ The hardware rule that shapes the fix — and the one choice we get to make The fast counter is private to a block — 256 cooks sharing 48 KB — and nobody outside the block can touch it. So a stage can escape the warehouse on one condition: all its pairs must sit inside data one block can gather onto its counter . The group size is ours to choose; the port picks 256 : counter budget: 48 KB ÷ 8 bytes per value = up to 6,144 values per group choose: 256 values (= 2 KB of the 48) — and 65,536 = 256 × 256 Why 256 exactly? It must be a power of two , so groups always contain whole pair-groups with nothing straddling an edge. And at N = 65,536 it makes the bookkeeping symmetric: 256 groups of 256 values , twice over — once strided, once contiguous (rung ④). A 2 KB counter also leaves room for many blocks per SM side by side (chapter 2's table: hundreds resident). one block's counter budget: 48 KB 2 KB spare — 46 KB of the allowance unused one SM station — neighbors bring their own tiles: 2 KB group block A 2 KB group block B 2 KB group block C ④ That number is the pair distance d Look at a pair's addresses when the list is viewed as a 256×256 grid (row = 256q + r): partners of a far stage (d a multiple of 256) have the same r — same column, different row — so each strided group {r, r+256, r+512, …} owns all far stages. Partners of a near stage (d ≤ 128) sit in the same row — a contiguous 256-tile owns all near stages. Two groupings, no third case. Stated cleanly, the four steps compress into one rule — the one structural idea of this port: the two-pass split · groups of 256, twice PASS 1 — the strided groups (d = 32,768 … 256) → 256 groups {r, r+256, …} each gather to a counter, run 8 stages, scatter PASS 2 — the contiguous tiles (d = 128 … 1) → 256 tiles of 256 each gather, run 8 stages, scatter Both passes run the same butterflies as the CPU reference. Pass 1 handles far pairs; pass 2 handles near pairs. This is four logical value movements, but pass 1 currently uses strided, uncoalesced addresses, so the hardware may issue many more memory transactions. 05 Keep a group in shared memory Global memory is the warehouse; shared memory is the counter. A shared-phase block does exactly four things: one block, one group · the kernel's whole life VRAM (global) the polynomial BLOCK — 256 cooks x = group id · y = limb 0..2 the block's COUNTER — 2 KB 256 values · 1 fetch in + 1 write out, total 1 2 4 3 8 stages · d = 128…1 · barrier each ① 256 cooks gather 256 values (1 each) · ② roll call — values land on the counter · ③ eight butterfly stages, barrier between · ④ carry the results back Naive code reads and writes VRAM at every stage. The two-pass design loads and stores each group once per pass. That reduces logical traffic, but pass 1 still needs a coalesced transpose or Four-Step layout to make those accesses efficient. A 256-value group uses 2 KB of shared memory per limb, leaving room for several blocks to reside on an SM. Actual occupancy on the RTX 5090 must be measured after register use and launch limits are known. The same trick, taken twice Notice what the tile trick actually was: a group of 2^k values hosts the k smallest-distance stages with zero outside communication . The port takes this trick twice — once with strided groups, once with contiguous ones — and that is the whole two-pass split: one forward at N = 65,536 · two passes, four truck trips PASS 1 strided groups {r, r+256, …} × 256 groups × 3 limbs 8 stages d = 32,768…256 8 stages on its counter 8 stages on its counter VRAM — the warehouse · the mix: pass 1 scatters strided, pass 2 gathers contiguous 8 stages d = 128…1 8 stages on its counter 8 stages on its counter PASS 2 contiguous tiles 256q … 256q+255 × 256 tiles × 3 limbs 1 2 3 4 per value: ① fetch + ② write-back + ③ fetch + ④ write-back = 4 warehouse trips — versus 16 naive Two things this shape fixes at once. The order differs from stage order only in grouping — the forward runs pass 1 then pass 2, the inverse runs the same ladder backwards. And every launch is self-contained: two kernel launches per forward (one per pass), each block needing nothing but its own 256 values. 06 Map the design to code Everything above exists in the repo in three small pieces. First, the butterfly body itself — written once , in include/ntt/dev_core.hpp , with the loop arranged as "one cook's slice of the pairs": // one DIF stage, one thread's slice — the same body the CPU simulator runs NTT_DEV void dev_dif_stage (uint64_t* tile, uint64_t tile_len, uint64_t d, uint64_t n, const uint64_t* pp, uint64_t q, uint32_t tid, uint32_t nthr) { const uint64_t lg = log2_of_pow2(d); for (uint64_t p = tid; p < tile_len / 2 ; p += nthr) { // MY pairs: start at my // thread id, stride by the thread count — chapter 3's disjoint pairs const uint64_t g = p >> lg, j = p & (d - 1 ); // which group, which offset const uint64_t u = (g << (lg + 1 )) + j, v = u + d; // the pair's two slots const uint64_t x = tile[u]; const uint64_t cv = mul_mod(pp[d], tile[v], q); // ladder constant ψ^d tile[u] = add_mod(x, cv, q); tile[v] = mul_mod(sub_mod(x, cv, q), pp[(n >> lg) * j], q); // twiddle } } Second, the pass-1 kernel — pure choreography around the stage bodies, in src/cuda/ntt_kernels.cu . One block owns one strided group, start to finish: __global__ void dif_col_kernel (uint64_t* a, const uint64_t* pp, const uint64_t* q, uint64_t n, uint32_t sub) { extern __shared__ uint64_t smem[]; // the counter const uint64_t r = blockIdx.x; // x = which strided group uint64_t* al = a + ( uint64_t )blockIdx.y * n; // y = which limb for (uint32_t t = threadIdx.x; t < sub; t += blockDim.x) // ① gather: value r+256t, smem[t] = al[r + ( uint64_t (t) << 8 )]; // one per cook __syncthreads(); // ② roll call for (uint64_t delta = sub / 2 ; delta >= 1 ; delta >>= 1 ) { // ③ the 8 far stages, dev_dif_col_stage(smem, sub, delta, n, pp, q, threadIdx.x, blockDim.x, r); __syncthreads(); // barrier each } for (uint32_t t = threadIdx.x; t < sub; t += blockDim.x) // ④ scatter back strided al[r + ( uint64_t (t) << 8 )] = smem[t]; } The pass-2 kernel ( dif_tile_kernel ) is the same shape with a contiguous gather — it is this kernel with r + (t<<8) replaced by base + t , running the near stages with dev_dif_stage . Third, the launches — where the grid's two addresses become the map of the whole problem. Remember RNS from the butterfly guide: the same transform runs once per limb (per prime), completely independently, so the y address is the limb: // one forward = TWO launches (grid = x × limbs): dif_col_kernel<<< dim3 ( 256 , num_limbs), T, sub * sizeof (uint64_t)>>>(buf, d_pp, d_q, n, sub); dif_tile_kernel<<< dim3 (n/ 256 , num_limbs), T, 256 * sizeof (uint64_t)>>>(buf, d_pp, d_q, n, 256 ); // pass 1: block (x=r, y=k) = strided group r of limb k — owns {r, r+256, …} // pass 2: block (x=q, y=k) = contiguous tile q of limb k — owns 256q … 256q+255 Three limbs means the GPU runs the entire RNS transform as one wave of blocks — no loop over limbs anywhere on the host. And the communication between stages — the part that makes or breaks a GPU program — is different in each phase, by design: ⇄ Between the two passes: the mix is pure data movement Pass 2's inputs are pass 1's outputs, regrouped — strided scatter becomes contiguous gather. No thread waits on another explicitly: the two launches share one stream, and pass 2 cannot begin until pass 1's writes have landed in VRAM. The pass boundary and the kernel boundary are the same line. ⇄ Between stages inside a pass: the barrier, because partners swap On the counter, the values your thread reads at stage d were written at stage 2d by different threads of your block — the crossing re-shuffles ownership every stage. That is the entire reason for __syncthreads() after each stage: all 256 cooks finish, then anyone may read. ∅ Between blocks: silence — and that is the design Inside either pass, every block's 256 values are a self-contained problem — a strided group for pass 1, a tile for pass 2 — and no pair ever leaves them. The forward has factorized into 768 independent mini-transforms per pass that never communicate, which is why one launch finishes eight whole stages , and why the GPU can pack blocks onto SMs in any arrangement it likes. 07 Synchronize between stages Two GPU habits bite newcomers, and both are already handled in the kernel — know them when you read it. the roll call rule · why barriers sit between stages the barrier — nobody passes alone cook A — done early cook B — working cook C — nearly there cook D — the slowest waiting… still working all cross together — when D arrives time → a block is exactly as fast as its slowest thread — so keep everyone's work the same shape Rule 1: the barrier is all-or-nothing Every thread of a block must reach every __syncthreads() . Put one inside an if that only some threads take, and the others wait forever — a hung kernel. That is why our barriers sit between stage loops, never inside the pair loop: all 256 cooks finish their slice, then everyone crosses together. Rule 2: idle cooks still attend roll call At N = 64 the tile is 64 values — only 32 pairs — but the block still has 256 threads. Most cooks hold no pair. Their loop body simply does zero iterations ( for (p = tid; p < 32; p += 256) never starts), and they walk straight to the barrier. Harmless — as long as they don't skip it . The repo's n=64 test fixture exists precisely to keep this edge honest. 08 Memory movement sets the pace The whole design — tiles, phases, staging — is really one decision: which shelf does each number live on? The shelves differ by orders of magnitude: cost to fetch one value · relative, order-of-magnitude Log-scale bars — each gridline is ×10. Exact cycles vary by GPU generation; the gaps are what matter. In kitchen terms: registers are in your hands, shared is on your station's counter, global is the warehouse across town, and copying from the host computer is a delivery truck. Our kernel's shape follows directly: start and end in the warehouse, stage the tile on the counter, keep loop counters and twiddles in hands — and never, ever truck data back and forth per stage. This ladder is also why the multiply pipeline stays on the GPU end to end: two forwards, pointwise, one inverse, then one truck trip home. 09 Current baseline and next optimizations Everything above is proven before any rental: the stage bodies live once in dev_core.hpp , compiled by a CPU simulator that must match the reference exactly — the rented GPU's gates then check only the thin kernel wrappers. One confession before you read the benchmarks: version 1 of the GPU arithmetic is deliberately unoptimized. The multiply inside every butterfly uses the same __uint128_t division as the CPU reference — because on the GPU that division is emulated : the hardware has no 128-bit divide, so the compiler builds one from ~a hundred instructions. Every butterfly pays it. That is the right order of operations: make it right, measure the gap, then make it fast . The bench table's job is to quantify exactly how slow v1 is — the CPU reference column is right there in the same table. The fix (Barrett or Montgomery reduction: division-free modular multiplication, the standard trick every production NTT uses) swaps in later behind the same function signature, with its own dedicated cross-check. The first RTX 5090 run answers one question: does every supported size match the reference exactly? Then benchmarks should isolate modular reduction, coalescing, radix, register pressure, and end-to-end transfer cost. The design in one paragraph Each thread computes butterfly pairs. Each block loads one group into shared memory, runs several stages with barriers, and writes the group back. A far-pair pass followed by a near-pair pass covers the full transform; x identifies the group and y identifies the RNS limb . The CPU simulator proves the schedule before GPU testing. The current baseline favors exact results over speed; optimization comes next through division-free modular reduction, coalesced data layout, higher radix, and device-resident pipelines. Start here if you haven't: Butterflies all the way down — why the NTT is butterflies at all.

title: Run & debug
summary: Run the N=8 example and step through each butterfly in VS Code.
text: Run and debug the NTT in VS Code ¶ This project checks in a shared VS Code configuration for macOS. The first debug target uses the CPU reference implementation, so CUDA hardware is not required. One-time setup ¶ Open the repository folder in VS Code: code . If VS Code asks, install the recommended extensions: - CMake Tools - C/C++ - LLDB DAP Wait for CMake Tools to finish configuring build/debug . The extensions are already installed on the current development Mac. The workspace explicitly uses Xcode's matching lldb-dap binary instead of CodeLLDB's bundled LLDB. Run the small example ¶ Open the command palette with Cmd+Shift+P , choose Tasks: Run Task , then choose Run: NTT debug example . The expected output is: natural-order coefficients: 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 bit-reversed evaluation values: 5 0 13 8 9 11 5 8 recovered coefficients: 1 2 3 4 5 6 7 8 roundtrip passed Debug it step by step ¶ Open examples/step_by_step.cpp . Click left of the transform.forward(values) line to create a breakpoint. Open Run and Debug with Cmd+Shift+D . Select Debug: NTT example (step by step) . Press F5 . The program first stops at main because stopOnEntry is on. Press F5 again to reach the breakpoint. Press F11 to step into NegacyclicNtt::forward in include/ntt/ntt.hpp . Use F10 to advance one source line at a time. Useful values to add to the Watch panel: stage_pair_distance group_start_index pair_offset upper_index lower_index twiddle_power values For N=8 , the forward transform has three stages with pair distances 4 , 2 , and 1 . Expand values after each butterfly to see the array change in place. Other shared commands ¶ Cmd+Shift+B : configure and build the debug example. Test: All CPU checks : build and run the complete CPU test suite. Debug: CPU unit tests : generate the N=1024 fixture and debug the tests. The debugger deliberately targets the CPU reference. CUDA kernel debugging will be added on the RTX machine using cuda-gdb or Nsight after the native CUDA build is available. CodeLLDB crash on current macOS/Xcode ¶ CodeLLDB 1.11.4's bundled LLDB 19.1.7 crashes with SIGBUS while parsing the Mach-O symbols produced by the current AppleClang toolchain. Xcode's native lldb-dap has been tested against this executable and stops at main correctly. If VS Code still shows a launch configuration with type lldb , run Developer: Reload Window and select the lldb-dap configuration again.

title: GPU NTT implementations
summary: Primary-source survey, performance limits, and techniques to evaluate.
text: GPU NTT survey for CKKS, Hybrid key switching, OpenFHE, and RTX 5090 ¶ Date: 2026-11-05 Project target: CKKS, OpenFHE 1.6.1, Hybrid RNS key switching, NVIDIA RTX 5090 ( sm_120 ), ring dimensions 4096..65536 Current repository revision inspected: 363f972 Evidence policy: implementation facts below come only from author papers, official repositories/source code, or NVIDIA documentation. Recommendations and inferences are explicitly labelled. Executive conclusions ¶ The current two-pass structure is a reasonable correctness scaffold, not yet a competitive GPU NTT. It has a valuable exact-reference contract, only two forward launches, shared-memory stage execution, and RNS-limb batching. Its principal performance blockers are device-side __uint128_t % q , severely strided global accesses in the column pass, a host-only synchronous API, and one fixed launch shape for all sizes and limb counts. FIDESlib is the most important comparison. It implements CKKS Hybrid key switching, targets OpenFHE 1.6.1, supports sm_120 , keeps CKKS objects on the GPU, fuses NTT/INTT boundaries with rescale, ModDown, and key-switch dot products, and tests exact GPU/CPU ciphertext equality. It is substantially closer to this project's end goal than a standalone NTT benchmark. Use Shoup multiplication for precomputed twiddles first. Every butterfly has a known multiplier, making Shoup's precomputed quotient a natural replacement for division. Use a separate Barrett/Montgomery-style path for variable-by-variable pointwise products. Introduce lazy ranges only with explicit range proofs and boundary tests. Replace the fixed radix-2-per-thread inner loop with multi-butterfly thread work. The strongest CKKS implementations hold 4 or 8 values in registers per thread, perform radix-4/radix-8 local work, exchange through padded shared memory, and reduce synchronization and twiddle traffic. Treat global layout and key-switch scheduling as first-class design decisions. On RTX 5090, recent analysis finds optimized NTT and basis-conversion kernels limited by L2/write bandwidth. The current column gather uses a 2,048-byte stride between neighboring threads' 64-bit loads at N >= 512 , so nominal byte counts understate the actual memory-transaction cost. Do not optimize NTT in isolation. The target unit is the GPU-resident Hybrid key-switch sequence: inverse NTT/decomposition, basis extension, forward NTT, evaluation-key multiply-accumulate, and basis reduction. Fuse safe producer/consumer boundaries and retain the extended QP representation when the OpenFHE operation sequence allows it. Benchmark both latency and throughput. A single ciphertext may underfill a 5090. Report kernel-only and end-to-end latency, batched tower/ciphertext throughput, memory traffic, achieved bandwidth, occupancy, and the complete key-switch/rotation latency. Always attach device, clocks, toolkit, driver, modulus bits, tower count, ordering, and transfer policy. 1. Current implementation: what it does well and where it differs from the literature ¶ 1.1 Sourced facts from this repository ¶ The CUDA backend uses a negacyclic transform with folded twisting and the following schedule: Forward: DIF column pass followed by a DIF contiguous-tile pass. Inverse: DIT contiguous-tile pass followed by a DIT column pass and a separate scale kernel. Fixed split width and block size of 256. Limb-major storage [limb][coefficient] ; blockIdx.y selects the limb. One full table of powers of psi and psi^-1 , each [limb][N+1] . Two launches per forward transform for N > 256 ; three for inverse. Host upload and download on every public forward , inverse , and pointwise_multiply call; multiply at least keeps its two forward transforms, pointwise product, and inverse together on device. Device multiplication is currently (__uint128_t(a) * b) % q . CPU simulation shares the exact stage bodies with CUDA, and CUDA tests compare exact arrays to a CPU reference and Python big-integer oracle. Primary code: ntt_kernels.cu , dev_core.hpp , mod_arith.hpp , and cuda_ntt.hpp . 1.2 Strengths worth retaining ¶ Recommendation/inference: keep these properties through optimization: The exact mathematical contract: natural-order input, bit-reversed evaluation output, exact inverse, and exact equality to the CPU oracle. The shared simulator/device stage definitions where practical. Optimized arithmetic can sit behind a second policy while the reference policy remains unchanged. Limb-major RNS storage as the baseline. It maps naturally to one modulus per independent transform, pointwise CKKS arithmetic, and OpenFHE's DCRT-tower model. Precomputation at context construction rather than in a hot operation. Named-hardware benchmark provenance and automatic correctness gates. 1.3 Immediate limitations ¶ Repository fact: mul_mod performs 128-bit remainder on every device multiply. The source itself marks this as a correctness-first, pre-Barrett implementation. Recommendation/inference: this must be replaced before NTT timing says anything useful. A radix-2 butterfly currently performs two modular products in this formulation, so division emulation dominates any memory-layout comparison. Repository fact: in dif_col_kernel , neighboring threads access a[r + 256*t] . For 64-bit coefficients, adjacent threads are separated by 2,048 bytes. The scatter has the same pattern. Recommendation/inference: this is the largest structural memory concern. Although the algorithm moves each coefficient through global memory only once per pass, the column pass is not warp-coalesced. Measure actual DRAM sectors and L2 transactions; do not describe the implementation as “four round-trips” without also reporting transaction efficiency. Repository fact: the tile and column kernels fetch twiddles from a full global table inside each stage, and synchronize the whole block after every radix-2 stage. Recommendation/inference: stage-major twiddle packing, precomputed Shoup quotients, register-held radix-4/8 work, warp shuffles for the smallest distances, and padded shared-memory exchange are the highest-value inner-kernel experiments. Repository fact: every transform uses 256 threads and a 256-way split, independent of N , modulus count, register pressure, shared-memory use, and GPU architecture. Recommendation/inference: replace the single hard-coded shape with a small, benchmarked dispatch table for N = 2^12..2^16 and for low/high tower counts. Compile-time specialization for five supported sizes is reasonable and permits unrolling and constant launch geometry. Repository fact: the public interface accepts host std::vector objects and uses synchronous cudaMemcpy ; it has no stream, device-buffer, external allocator, or graph-capture contract. Recommendation/inference: retain this API as a convenience/reference facade, but add a device-resident API before OpenFHE integration. Otherwise host transfers and forced synchronization will erase key-switch gains. 2. Representative implementations and transferable techniques ¶ 2.1 FIDESlib: the closest match to the project target ¶ FIDESlib describes itself as a server-side CKKS GPU library interoperable with OpenFHE. Its current release states support for OpenFHE 1.6.1, Hybrid key switching, CUDA 12/13, and sm_70 through sm_120 ; it also states that GPU operations are compared bit-for-bit to a patched OpenFHE CPU reference. These are precisely this project's scheme, integration, key-switch, and GPU targets. See the official README and its bit-compatibility design record . Its current 1D NTT uses CT butterflies for forward and GS butterflies for inverse, shared-memory staging, warp-level synchronization below a warp, vectorized 16-byte loads/stores, and Shoup/Barrett arithmetic selected by templates. More importantly, the NTT mode is templated to fuse downstream work including rescale, plaintext multiplication, ModDown, and key-switch dot/accumulate operations. See NTT_1D.cu , INTT_1D.cu , NTTfusions.cuh , and ModMult.cuh . FIDESlib's Hybrid pipeline has dedicated decomposition/ModUp and ModDown kernels, per-device limb partitions, CUDA streams/events, and graph capture in its multi-GPU/scheduling layer. Its high-level RNS object tracks whether a polynomial is in the extended basis and exposes fused key-switch operations. See Conv.cu , LimbPartition.cu , and RNSPoly.cpp . What to absorb: Make exact OpenFHE ciphertext compatibility—not only decrypt-level CKKS tolerance—the integration acceptance target where the same algorithmic formulation is used. Model transform state explicitly: coefficient/evaluation order, normal/extended RNS basis, level, and owning device/stream. Create fusion points at transform boundaries. A generic forward() that always stores a complete intermediate is insufficient for high-performance key switching. Use Shoup constants beside twiddle and key constants. Keep generic Barrett reduction for operands whose multiplier is not precomputed. Test the complete Hybrid formulations. FIDESlib's compatibility record shows that two mathematically valid rotation/key-switch formulations need not produce bit-identical ciphertexts because rounding and noise enter in different orders. Preserve full QP towers during export/import. FIDESlib documents a real compatibility bug caused by truncating extended-basis ciphertexts during materialization. Inference: FIDESlib is both a design reference and a competitor baseline. Before designing a new OpenFHE patch layer, evaluate whether this project's intended contribution is (a) independent kernels integrated directly into stock OpenFHE, (b) an alternative backend with a stable ABI, or (c) improvements that can be contributed to FIDESlib/OpenFHE. Duplicating its entire compatibility layer without a differentiator is high effort. 2.2 GPU-NTT / HEonGPU: Merge NTT and Four-Step NTT ¶ Özcan and Savaş present two GPU algorithms: an iterative “Merge NTT” and a Four-Step NTT. Their target ranges include 2^12..2^16 for HE and larger sizes for proving. They optimize kernel count and block shape for coalesced global access, and report both single-transform latency and concurrent-transform throughput. The paper reports that the iterative form can outperform Four-Step for HE throughput despite Four-Step's locality. See the author paper, Two Algorithms for Fast GPU Implementation of NTT , especially its design and evaluation sections. The current official GPU-NTT repository supports 32- and 64-bit Barrett arithmetic, rejecting moduli above 30 and 61 bits respectively. It specializes ring sizes at compile time, uses per-size kernel configuration tables, supports RNS transforms and batches, accepts CUDA streams, and has different low-ring and multi-stage paths. See the official repository , ntt_launch_impl.cuh , and modular_arith.cuh . HEonGPU uses GPU-NTT inside a GPU-resident BFV/CKKS library. Its paper describes a GPU memory pool, pinned host pool, and multi-stream execution in addition to the NTT itself. See HEonGPU and the official repository . What to absorb: Compare at least two schedules: an improved two-pass/Merge path and a Four-Step or explicit transpose path. Do not assume the current fixed split is optimal. Build a per-size launch table. The supported range is only five powers of two, so exhaustive offline tuning on the 5090 is tractable. Treat batches as part of the NTT API, not a benchmark wrapper. CKKS naturally supplies many modulus towers and often multiple ciphertext components. Report throughput as well as latency; the best shape changes when enough independent transforms exist to saturate the GPU. Add an allocator and stream contract at the library boundary. 2.3 CKKS-GPU-CORE: memory-centric CKKS and 8-point-per-thread NTT ¶ Jung et al.'s memory-centric CKKS work keeps up to eight NTT values per thread in registers, exchanges through shared memory between local subtransforms, and pads shared memory to reduce bank conflicts. Its basis conversion launches across output limbs and coefficients and accumulates input-limb products before Barrett reduction. See Over 100x Faster Bootstrapping in Fully Homomorphic Encryption through Memory-Centric Optimization with GPUs and the official CKKS-GPU-CORE repository . The source implements two NTT phases, register arrays of eight coefficients per thread, Shoup butterflies, padded shared memory, batched ModUp, and fused ModDown/NTT epilogues. See NttImple.cu and Context.cu . What to absorb: Evaluate radix-8-per-thread as a direct evolution of this repository's two-pass structure: keep eight coefficients in registers, use shared memory only for cross-thread permutations, and reduce full-block barriers. Add padding and profile bank conflicts rather than assuming the [256] shared tile is conflict-free for every access pattern. Co-design basis conversion and NTT buffers. The same extended-basis layout should flow directly into forward NTT and evaluation-key multiplication. Fuse inverse-transform epilogues and forward-transform prologues where the Hybrid formula permits. 2.4 PhantomFHE: radix-8 NWT, lazy Shoup butterflies, and scheme-level fusion ¶ Phantom implements BFV, BGV, and CKKS on CUDA. Its 1D path handles small transforms in one block; its larger 2D path performs radix-8 work with eight register-held values per thread, padded shared-memory exchanges, and two phases. Forward CT butterflies use Shoup multiplication and lazy [0, 2q) / [0, 4q) ranges; inverse GS butterflies defer final reduction/scaling. See the official repository , ntt_1d.cu , fntt_2d.cu , and butterfly.cuh . The Phantom paper describes intra-kernel fusion that reuses register temporaries and inter-kernel fusion across operations such as NWT plus scaling and ModDown plus correction. Its key-switch path connects ModUp, evaluation-key inner product, and ModDown on a supplied stream. See Phantom: A CUDA-Accelerated Word-Wise Homomorphic Encryption Library and eval_key_switch.cu . What to absorb: Use CT forward and GS inverse so compatible orderings can eliminate explicit permutations between NTT, pointwise multiplication, and INTT. Define and prove lazy ranges per butterfly. Reductions are removed only when the next consumer's bound remains safe. Prefer register reuse and boundary fusion over simply increasing shared-memory tile size. Expose the CUDA stream all the way through key switching. 2.5 TensorFHE: tensor-core NTT and operation-level batching ¶ TensorFHE maps a decomposed 32-bit NTT to tensor-core matrix multiplications and emphasizes throughput rather than single-operation latency. It batches CKKS operations and changes layout from (batch, limb, N) to (limb, batch, N) so equal-limb data from different operations is contiguous. It also assigns independent matrix multiplications to separate streams. See the author paper, TensorFHE , especially Sections IV-C and IV-D. What to absorb: Operation-level batching and a layout selectable between [limb][batch][N] and [batch][limb][N] are worth measuring for inference serving. Throughput-oriented inference can benefit from batching several ciphertexts even if one ciphertext already batches all RNS towers. Inference/caution: do not make tensor-core NTT the first implementation path. TensorFHE's arithmetic decomposition and throughput objective differ from OpenFHE's usual 50–60-bit RNS towers and this project's immediate exact-compatibility goal. Establish a fast integer-core Shoup/Barrett backend first; treat tensor cores as a separate experimental backend. 2.6 ICICLE: useful API ideas, not a direct CKKS backend ¶ ICICLE's official NTT API exposes stream, batch size, row/column batch layout, input/output ordering, device-resident flags, async execution, reusable per-device domains, fast-twiddle mode, and an explicit mixed-radix selection. See the official NTT API . What to absorb: Separate an algorithm-independent NTT contract from backend-specific tuning extensions. Make ordering explicit in the type/configuration rather than relying on comments. Initialize and cache a maximum-size domain once, then reuse it for smaller transforms where mathematically compatible. Allow both row-batched and column-batched transforms and device-resident async operation. Inference/caution: ICICLE is primarily a proof-system field library, not an OpenFHE CKKS/Hybrid implementation. Its API concepts transfer; its field choices and transform semantics must not be assumed compatible. Its CUDA backend also has source-availability/licensing conditions that should be checked before any reuse. 2.7 cuFHE/cuHE: historically relevant but not the integration model ¶ cuFHE implements TFHE gates and credits cuHE's GPU NTT; its API supports CUDA streams and keeps a public bootstrapping key initialized on the GPU. See the official cuFHE repository and official cuHE repository . What to absorb: Keep large evaluation/bootstrapping keys resident and permit concurrent independent operations through streams. Inference/caution: TFHE gate bootstrapping has different polynomial sizes, dataflow, and key-switch structure from CKKS Hybrid RNS. cuFHE is not a suitable algorithmic baseline for the OpenFHE integration; it is mainly historical evidence for GPU-resident keys and stream-level concurrency. 2.8 Theodosian: RTX 5090 changes the optimization priority ¶ Theodosian profiles CKKS on RTX 5090 and reports that optimized NTT and basis-conversion kernels are L2-bandwidth-bound. Its NTT uses two kernels; on-the-fly twiddle generation trades arithmetic for fewer twiddle loads. It finds small limb counts underutilize the GPU, uses L2-aware batching until the working set approaches cache capacity, applies multi-polynomial caching and complementary pipelining to Hybrid key-switch stages, and uses CUDA Graphs to reduce launch overhead for static FHE graphs. See Theodosian . The paper reports that batching can hurt after the footprint exceeds the 5090's effective L2 capacity, and that key switching benefits more from cache-aware multi-polynomial execution and graph scheduling than from additional local kernel fusion once the baseline is already heavily fused. What to absorb: Profile L2 read/write throughput and SM-to-L2 traffic on the actual 5090, not only DRAM bandwidth and occupancy. Generate high-volume twiddles on the fly when the arithmetic cost is cheaper than their cache traffic; retain a precomputed mode for low-volume stages. Batch according to measured working-set size. “More batches” is not monotonic. Capture stable key-switch/rotation/inference sequences in CUDA Graphs. Pipeline stages with complementary DRAM/L2 behavior only after dependencies and cache interference are measured. 3. Algorithm and arithmetic choices for this project ¶ 3.1 CT/GS versus Stockham and Four-Step ¶ Sourced observation: Phantom and FIDESlib use CT forward plus GS inverse; GPU-NTT compares iterative Merge and Four-Step schedules; ICICLE exposes mixed-radix and ordering choices. Recommendation: keep CT/DIF forward and GS/DIT inverse as the first optimized path because the current repository already has the equivalent ordering contract and no bit-reversal pass. Add a Four-Step/transpose prototype only as a benchmarked alternative for the strided column pass. A Stockham autosort path may offer regular accesses and natural ordering, but it normally ping-pongs global buffers; for the target sizes, its extra full-array traffic must beat the cost of the current uncoalesced gather before adoption. 3.2 Mixed radix and register staging ¶ Sourced observation: CKKS-GPU-CORE and Phantom use up to eight values per thread and radix-8 local transforms; GPU-NTT notes higher-radix butterflies as a further optimization. Recommendation: implement radix-4 first, then radix-8: Load 4/8 values per thread using coalesced vectorized transactions. Execute the local stages in registers. Store into padded shared memory for the permutation between local groups. Use warp shuffles where partner lanes remain within a warp. Store once at the end of the phase. This directly reduces table loads, barriers, and shared-memory operations relative to one butterfly per thread per stage. 3.3 Modular multiplication ¶ Sourced observation: GPU-NTT uses Barrett with explicit modulus-bit bounds; Phantom and CKKS-GPU-CORE use Shoup values for twiddles and lazy butterflies; FIDESlib provides Shoup and Barrett paths. Recommendation: use three explicit primitives rather than one universal mul_mod : mul_const_shoup(x, w, w_shoup, q) for twiddles, N^-1 , basis constants, and evaluation-key constants when precomputation is useful. mul_var_barrett(a, b, q, mu) or a benchmarked Montgomery alternative for pointwise variable products. reduce_wide(acc, q, mu) for basis-conversion/key-switch accumulators with a proved accumulator bound. Retain the current __uint128_t % q only as host/device test oracle. Test each optimized primitive exhaustively around 0 , q-1 , lazy bounds, and the maximum supported OpenFHE prime size. 3.4 Twiddle representation ¶ Recommendation/inference: replace [psi^0, ..., psi^N] as the only device representation with: stage/phase-major twiddles in the order consumed by warps; a parallel Shoup quotient table; optional compact “seed” twiddles for on-the-fly expansion in the phase with O(N) table traffic; a metadata record containing transform convention, direction, modulus, ordering, and supported lazy range. The CPU reference can continue to build a simple power table; a packing step should produce the device format and be independently cross-checked. 4. RNS data layout and Hybrid key-switch implications ¶ 4.1 Baseline layout ¶ Recommendation: keep coefficient data limb-major: poly[component][digit-or-batch][limb][coefficient] with coefficient contiguous. This gives coalesced coefficient loads for one limb and makes modulus-specific constants uniform across a block. Provide views/strides so operation-level batching can switch the middle dimensions without copying. 4.2 Extended-basis state ¶ Recommendation: make these states explicit and non-interchangeable: Q, coefficient Q, evaluation QP, coefficient QP, evaluation Each buffer view should carry active Q tower count, P tower count, level, ordering, device, and stream/event ownership. This prevents accidental truncation or redundant transforms at the OpenFHE boundary. 4.3 Target Hybrid pipeline ¶ Recommendation/inference: design the first end-to-end kernel graph around OpenFHE's actual Hybrid formulation, approximately: input c2 in Q/evaluation -> digit partition / inverse NTT as required -> Q-digit to QP basis extension -> forward NTT of extended digits -> evaluation-key multiply-accumulate into two QP outputs -> approximate ModDown QP -> Q -> add/fold c0 as required by the exact OpenFHE operation The exact transform placement and rounding order must be derived from the pinned OpenFHE 1.6.1 source and frozen in compatibility tests. Do not substitute an algebraically equivalent formulation if bit equality is the goal. 4.4 Fusion candidates ¶ High-value, low-ambiguity experiments: INTT final scaling + decomposition pre-scale. Basis-extension output + first forward-NTT load/prologue. Forward-NTT final store + evaluation-key dot product when register and occupancy costs permit. INTT or NTT boundary + ModDown correction. Pointwise accumulation across Hybrid digits, deferring reduction only under a proved bound. Caution: fusion can lower occupancy by increasing registers/shared memory and can prevent cache-friendly scheduling. Theodosian shows additional fusion is not automatically beneficial on RTX 5090. Require profiler evidence for every fused variant. 5. Streams, transfers, allocation, and launch strategy ¶ NVIDIA documents that asynchronous host/device copies require pinned host memory and can overlap with kernels in other streams. It also documents global-to-shared asynchronous copies and pipelines, and states that CUDA Graphs reduce repeated launch setup cost for fixed workflows. See the CUDA Best Practices Guide , asynchronous copy documentation , and CUDA Graphs documentation . Recommended API split: NttContext : immutable moduli, roots, packed twiddles, reduction constants, launch table, and allocator handle. DeviceRnsView : pointer(s), dimensions/strides, basis/domain/order metadata, device, and readiness event. enqueue_forward/inverse(view, stream) : no allocation, no synchronization, no host copy. convenience host methods: pinned staging plus explicit or documented synchronization. reusable scratch arena sized for maximum supported level/digit count. captured CUDA graphs for fixed ring dimension, level, digit count, and operation sequence. Recommendation/inference: try cuda::memcpy_async /pipeline only after the coalesced phase layout is fixed. The current column gather has no useful sequential “next tile” per block to hide without first changing data ownership; async copy cannot repair uncoalesced addresses. 6. Correctness and benchmark methodology ¶ 6.1 Correctness ladder ¶ Arithmetic primitive versus __uint128_t % q , including adversarial bounds and every OpenFHE modulus. Butterfly and single-stage exact tests for CT/DIF and GS/DIT, including lazy-range invariants. Complete forward/inverse exact equality against the existing CPU and Python oracle for every N in {4096, 8192, 16384, 32768, 65536} . RNS batches across realistic CKKS tower counts, not only three limbs. Negacyclic polynomial multiplication exact equality. Basis conversion exact equality to the pinned OpenFHE 1.6.1 implementation. Hybrid relinearization and rotation: exact ciphertext comparison where formulation and code generation permit; decrypt-error comparison as a secondary semantic test. Long operation sequences and inference circuits, including level/scale/noise metadata and repeated rotations. 6.2 Required performance views ¶ For each ring dimension, modulus bit-width, and tower count: kernel-only forward and inverse latency using CUDA events; end-to-end latency with pinned and pageable host transfer reported separately; transforms/second for batches of towers, ciphertext components, and independent ciphertexts; full polynomial multiply latency; Hybrid key switch, relinearization, and rotation latency; complete inference latency and peak device memory; bytes read/written, achieved DRAM bandwidth, L2 read/write throughput, global load/store efficiency, bank conflicts, register count, occupancy, and launch count from Nsight Compute/Systems; cold setup, warm steady state, and CUDA Graph replay as distinct measurements. 6.3 Baselines ¶ This repository's current pre-Barrett kernel, labelled clearly as a correctness baseline. Optimized kernel with identical transfers. GPU-NTT or another standalone GPU NTT with matched modulus/order/batch where license and semantics permit. FIDESlib 2.2/OpenFHE 1.6.1 for NTT microbenchmarks and, more importantly, full Hybrid key switch/rotation. Stock OpenFHE 1.6.1 CPU, with build flags and thread count recorded. Do not compare one implementation's kernel-only time with another's transfer-inclusive time, nor one-limb latency with an entire RNS polynomial. 7. Prioritized points to absorb ¶ P0: required before meaningful performance work ¶ Add Shoup twiddle multiplication and a variable-product Barrett/Montgomery path. Add exact arithmetic gates for the maximum OpenFHE modulus width. Add a device-resident, stream-aware API. Benchmark the current column pass's memory-transaction efficiency on RTX 5090. Pin OpenFHE 1.6.1 and extract its exact Hybrid transform/order/basis contract into tests. P1: first competitive NTT ¶ Implement per-size compile-time dispatch for 2^12..2^16 . Implement radix-4/8 register staging with padded shared memory. Pack stage-major twiddle and Shoup tables. Prototype a coalesced transpose/Four-Step alternative to the strided column pass. Benchmark latency and RNS/ciphertext throughput; choose by size and batch, not one universal kernel. P2: base conversion and Hybrid key switching ¶ Freeze the limb-major Q/QP device layout and explicit domain/basis metadata. Implement basis conversion with output-limb × coefficient parallelism and bounded wide accumulators. Fuse selected NTT/basis/key-dot boundaries. Keep evaluation keys and scratch buffers resident. Add CUDA Graph capture for relinearization and rotation. P3: inference-oriented optimization ¶ Add operation-level batching with an L2-capacity guard. Hoist decomposition for groups of rotations. Reuse extended-basis results across compatible operations. Profile complementary stream pipelines and whole-model memory traffic.
