Consider 32-bit/tensor-core research only as an optional backend because it changes OpenFHE parameter representation and compatibility assumptions. 8. Licensing and clean-room implementation ¶ This section is informational, not legal advice. FIDESlib: MIT license in its official repository. Its OpenFHE interoperability currently depends on patches, which should be reviewed separately for upstream/license provenance. GPU-NTT: Apache-2.0. HEonGPU: check the repository's current license before copying code; concepts described by the paper can be independently implemented. PhantomFHE: GPLv3. Copying its source into a differently licensed project can impose copyleft obligations. Use the paper and behavior as design evidence unless the project intentionally adopts compatible licensing. CKKS-GPU-CORE: CC BY-NC-SA 4.0 in the repository. The non-commercial/share-alike terms make direct code reuse unsuitable for many projects. Independently implement paper-level ideas and preserve clean-room provenance. ICICLE CUDA backend: source availability and the backend license have changed across releases. Verify the exact version's terms before any reuse. cuFHE/cuHE: their official repositories state their licenses; verify individual files before reuse. Recommendation: continue the repository's clean-room policy. Cite papers and inspect behavior/interfaces, but write original kernels. If code is adapted from MIT/Apache sources, preserve required notices and record the exact file/commit. Do not copy GPL or CC BY-NC-SA kernel code unless the project's license decision explicitly permits it. 9. Decision summary for the next code update ¶ The survey supports the following immediate implementation sequence: Introduce arithmetic policies and implement ShoupTwiddle plus BarrettVariable , with exact tests. Add a device-buffer/stream API without removing the current host-vector facade. Instrument and benchmark the existing two-pass kernel on RTX 5090 using CUDA events and Nsight. Implement one radix-8, padded-shared-memory variant and one coalesced transpose/Four-Step variant. Select per-size/per-batch winners through a dispatch table. Build the Q/QP state/layout and OpenFHE 1.6.1 compatibility harness before implementing base conversion. Optimize and report the full Hybrid key-switch graph, with FIDESlib as the central GPU baseline. Benchmarking and autotuning across GPU parameters and implementation variants are a permanent project workstream, not a one-time comparison. The concrete matrix, required counters, reproducibility record, dispatch rules, and acceptance gates are defined in benchmark-tuning-plan.md . The HTML explainer should then be updated to show both the current correctness schedule and the selected production schedule. It should no longer imply that low nominal global byte count alone means efficient VRAM access; it should visualize coalescing, register-held radix-8 work, padded shared memory, and the complete Q -> QP -> Q Hybrid dataflow. Primary sources ¶ Özcan and Savaş, Two Algorithms for Fast GPU Implementation of NTT ; GPU-NTT source . Özcan and Savaş, HEonGPU ; HEonGPU source . Yang et al., Phantom ; PhantomFHE source . Jung et al., Over 100x Faster Bootstrapping through Memory-Centric Optimization with GPUs ; CKKS-GPU-CORE source . Fan et al., TensorFHE . Agulló-Domingo et al., FIDESlib source and documentation . Choi et al., Theodosian . Ingonyama, ICICLE NTT API . Vernam Lab, cuFHE and cuHE . NVIDIA, CUDA C++ Programming Guide , CUDA C++ Best Practices Guide , and Nsight Compute documentation .

title: Choosing the GPU
summary: Compare hardware for exact u32/u64 modular arithmetic and CKKS workloads.
text: GPU Selection Survey for CKKS NTT, Base Conversion, and Hybrid Key Switching ¶ Last updated: 2026-11-06 Status: initial hardware decision; validate with the benchmark gate below before purchase or long-term rental Decision ¶ Use the GeForce RTX 5090 as the primary development and optimization target. It is the strongest practical single-workstation choice for this project: Blackwell sm_120 , 32 GB of GDDR7, 1.792 TB/s peak memory bandwidth, 96 MB of L2, and 104.8 peak non-Tensor INT32 TOPS. NVIDIA lists a US starting price of $1,999 , although actual market prices vary. These characteristics are relevant to NTT/RNS work even though the card is also marketed heavily for FP4/FP8 AI. Use an RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell when 32 GB is proven insufficient or production reliability is required. It has the same 1.792 TB/s memory bandwidth but 96 GB of GDDR7 with ECC, 128 MB of L2, 24,064 CUDA cores, and 126 peak non-Tensor INT32 TOPS. The tradeoff is a much higher price and a 600 W board power limit. Do not choose H100/H200/B200 solely from AI Tensor-Core numbers. Their HBM capacity and bandwidth are excellent, but NVIDIA does not publish a directly comparable native INT64 modular-multiply throughput. They may win a memory-bound, large-batch production workload, but that is an inference that must be established by our kernels and profiler data. This is a provisional decision, not a claim that the RTX 5090 is universally fastest. The final selection must pass the cross-GPU benchmark gate in this report. Why FP8 and FP16 marketing does not answer our question ¶ Our hot operations are expected to be: u32 / u64 modular add and subtract; 32-by-32-to-64 and 64-by-64 product-high/product-low operations; Shoup or Barrett reduction; permutations, gathers, transposes, and RNS-tower traffic; shared-memory and register movement; base-conversion accumulation across Q and P towers. NVIDIA's Tensor Core input-type table lists FP64, TF32, BF16, FP16, FP8, FP6, FP4, INT8, and INT4. It does not list arbitrary u32 or u64 modular arithmetic. Therefore, FP8/FP16 Tensor TOPS are not a direct performance metric for our kernels. NVIDIA's PTX integer instruction documentation supports mul.hi , mul.lo , and mul.wide . The full-width .wide form exists only for 16- and 32-bit inputs. CUDA also exposes __umul64hi , which returns the high half of a 64-by-64-bit product. These are the relevant building blocks for Shoup/Barrett arithmetic. The CUDA Best Practices throughput table gives mad.lo.s32 a theoretical 64 results per cycle per SM for the listed architectures, with a footnote of 32 for extended-precision operations. It publishes a row for 64-bit integer addition, but no row for 64-bit integer multiplication . Consequently, any claim such as “GPU X has Y INT64 TOPS” would be unsupported by NVIDIA's public specifications. NVIDIA's RTX Blackwell whitepaper does state that the RTX Blackwell SM doubles integer-math throughput per clock compared with Ada and publishes peak non-Tensor INT32 totals. This is useful evidence for the RTX 5090, but it still does not replace measurement of our multi-instruction modular multiplication. Official specification comparison ¶ INT32 below means the published non-Tensor peak when NVIDIA provides one. It must not be read as INT64 or modular-multiplication throughput. Not published is intentional; this report does not invent missing numbers. GPU Architecture / CC Memory Peak bandwidth Official L2 ECC / reliability statement Power Published non-Tensor INT32 CUDA support GeForce RTX 5090 RTX Blackwell GB202 / 12.0 32 GB GDDR7 1,792 GB/s 96 MB GDDR7 built-in single-bit correction is always enabled; not the same enterprise product/support proposition as RTX PRO/data-center cards 575 W TGP 104.8 TOPS CUDA 12.8+; compile sm_120 GeForce RTX 4090 Ada AD102 / 8.9 24 GB GDDR6X 1,008 GB/s 72 MB No product-level ECC feature published 450 W TGP 41.3 TOPS CUDA 11.8+; compile sm_89 RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation RTX Blackwell GB202 / 12.0 96 GB GDDR7 with ECC 1,792 GB/s 128 MB ECC, enterprise drivers/support, MIG 600 W board power 126.0 TOPS CUDA 12.8+; compile sm_120 L40S Ada / 8.9 48 GB GDDR6 with ECC 864 GB/s Not stated on the current L40S page; 96 MB is documented for L40/full AD102 ECC; designed for continuous data-center operation 350 W Not published for L40S CUDA 11.8+; compile sm_89 A100 80 GB SXM Ampere GA100 / 8.0 80 GB HBM2e 2,039 GB/s 40 MB HBM, L2, L1, and register-file ECC documented 400 W standard; selected systems up to 500 W 19.5 TOPS in NVIDIA's architecture comparison CUDA 11.0+; compile sm_80 H100 SXM Hopper GH100 / 9.0 80 GB HBM3 3.35 TB/s 50 MB Data-center HBM ECC/error-containment family Up to 700 W 30 TOPS in NVIDIA's architecture comparison CUDA 11.8+/12.x; compile sm_90 H200 SXM Hopper GH100 / 9.0 141 GB HBM3e 4.8 TB/s 50 MB Hopper L2 Data-center HBM ECC/error-containment family Up to 700 W Not published in current product sheet CUDA 11.8+/12.x; compile sm_90 B200 SXM Blackwell GB100 / 10.0 180 GB HBM3e Up to 8 TB/s 126 MB Data-center HBM ECC/error-containment family Configurable up to 1,000 W in HGX Not published for native INT32/INT64 modular arithmetic CUDA 12.8+; compile sm_100 Primary sources for the table ¶ NVIDIA's CUDA GPU compute-capability list maps RTX 5090 and RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell to CC 12.0, B200 to CC 10.0, H100/H200 to CC 9.0, RTX 4090/L40S to CC 8.9, and A100 to CC 8.0. NVIDIA's CUDA architecture/toolkit matrix lists first toolkit support and ongoing support; CUDA 12.8 added sm_100 , sm_101 , and sm_120 compiler support. The RTX Blackwell architecture whitepaper provides the RTX 5090's 170 SMs, 21,760 CUDA cores, 32 GB GDDR7, 1.792 TB/s, 96 MB L2, 575 W, 104.8 INT32 TOPS, and built-in GDDR7 single-bit correction. It also provides RTX 4090 comparison figures. The RTX PRO Blackwell architecture whitepaper provides 96 GB ECC GDDR7, 1.792 TB/s, 128 MB L2, 600 W, and 126 INT32 TOPS. The shorter product datasheet confirms the main board specifications. The official L40S product page specifies 48 GB GDDR6 with ECC, 864 GB/s, 18,176 CUDA cores, and 350 W. The Ada architecture whitepaper documents the 96 MB L2 full-AD102/L40 configuration; the current L40S page does not separately state L2. The A100 product page specifies 80 GB HBM2e, 2,039 GB/s for SXM, and 400 W. NVIDIA's Ampere architecture analysis documents 40 MB L2 and SECDED protection of HBM, L2, L1, and register files. The H100 datasheet specifies 80 GB, 3.35 TB/s, and up to 700 W. NVIDIA's Hopper architecture analysis documents 50 MB L2 and its architecture comparison. The H200 datasheet specifies 141 GB HBM3e, 4.8 TB/s, and up to 700 W. NVIDIA's HGX component table specifies H100/H200/B200 capacity and bandwidth and a configurable limit up to 1 kW per GPU. The Blackwell tuning guide documents B200/GB200's 180 GB memory support and 126 MB L2. NVIDIA's GPU memory-error management guide documents HBM ECC correction and error-management behavior for Ampere, Hopper, and Blackwell data-center families. Cost and availability snapshot ¶ Prices are volatile, regional, and not directly comparable between a bare card and a complete cloud VM. The following are official reference points, not a purchasing quote: NVIDIA lists the RTX 5090 from $1,999 . NVIDIA launched the RTX 4090 from $1,599 , but its current official product page no longer provides a meaningful live purchase price. A used or already-owned 4090 can still be economical; a new project should not assume launch-price availability. NVIDIA Marketplace listed a partner RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell Workstation Edition at $14,079.99 when this report was checked. That is about seven times the RTX 5090 list price for three times the VRAM, professional ECC positioning, MIG, enterprise support, and about 20% more published non-Tensor INT32 peak—not seven times the kernel performance. See the official NVIDIA Marketplace listing . Google Cloud lists an RTX PRO 6000 96 GB virtual-workstation GPU at $1.09565 per GPU-hour in the first displayed region, before the VM, storage, network, and any licensing charges. The page states that price and availability vary by region. See Google Cloud GPU pricing . AWS Capacity Blocks list examples of about $5.97 per H100-hour and $14.21–$14.80 per B200-hour , sold as eight-GPU blocks in the shown regions. These are suitable for bounded cross-GPU experiments, not evidence that either card is cost-effective for daily development. See AWS Capacity Blocks pricing . Inference: local RTX 5090 ownership is the best development economics when the card remains well utilized. A cloud RTX PRO 6000 is an attractive way to validate the 96 GB path without buying a workstation card. H200/B200 rentals should be delayed until optimized kernels and a fixed benchmark harness exist, otherwise expensive time will mostly measure unfinished code. Interpretation for this project ¶ 1. RTX 5090 versus RTX 4090 ¶ Fact: RTX 5090 has 1.78 times the peak memory bandwidth, 33% more memory capacity, 33% more L2, and about 2.54 times the published peak non-Tensor INT32 rate. Inference: it should be a materially better target for NTT, basis conversion, and key-switch kernels than RTX 4090. The actual speedup will be smaller or larger depending on whether the kernel is constrained by memory coalescing, extended-precision multiply chains, register pressure, or synchronization. The RTX 4090 remains useful as an Ada compatibility target and may be attractive if already owned. It should not be purchased as the project's primary new card without a major price advantage. 2. RTX 5090 versus RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell ¶ Fact: both have 1.792 TB/s peak memory bandwidth and CC 12.0. RTX PRO 6000 has 3 times the memory, 33% more L2, about 20% more published INT32 throughput, ECC positioning, and enterprise features. Inference: for a kernel whose working set fits in 32 GB, the RTX PRO 6000 is unlikely to offer a performance increase proportional to its price. It becomes the better choice when evaluation-key caching, batching, or multiple contexts exceeds 32 GB, or when long-running production reliability/support matters more than acquisition cost. 3. RTX 5090 versus A100/H100/H200/B200 ¶ Fact: the data-center GPUs offer larger ECC HBM and much more bandwidth: about 2.0 TB/s for A100, 3.35 TB/s for H100, 4.8 TB/s for H200, and up to 8 TB/s for B200. H100/H200/B200 also allow larger shared-memory allocations than CC 12.x RTX Blackwell: NVIDIA's Blackwell tuning guide states 228 KB physical capacity and 227 KB maximum per block for CC 10.0, versus 128 KB physical capacity and 99 KB maximum per block for CC 12.0. Fact: NVIDIA does not provide a current product-table value for native INT64 multiply throughput on any of them. Their headline FP8/FP16/INT8 Tensor performance does not measure our workload. Inference: H200 or B200 may be best for a large-batch, memory-bandwidth-bound production service, especially when evaluation keys exceed 32/96 GB or multiple key sets must stay resident. Conversely, RTX 5090 can outperform older data-center GPUs in compute-bound u32 work because its published non-Tensor INT32 peak is much higher. Only our modular-arithmetic microbenchmarks and end-to-end Hybrid key switching can settle the balance. 4. Is 32 GB enough? ¶ For a single RNS polynomial, storage is approximately: bytes = ring_dimension * active_towers * 8 At N = 65,536 , one polynomial with 40 towers is about 20 MiB. Ciphertext components alone therefore fit easily. Hybrid evaluation keys, QP temporaries, cached twiddle tables, concurrent ciphertexts, and model rotations can dominate the footprint. Inference: 32 GB is likely sufficient for development and many single-request CKKS inference cases, but it must not be assumed sufficient for the final application. We should add peak device-memory measurement to the OpenFHE integration tests before deciding whether production needs 48, 80, 96, 141, or 180 GB. Recommended acquisition strategy ¶ Primary local card: RTX 5090, if the machine can support its power and cooling requirements. Compatibility card: retain or rent an RTX 4090/L40S to ensure sm_89 remains correct and to quantify Blackwell-specific gains. Production-capacity candidate: RTX PRO 6000 Blackwell if the measured resident set exceeds 28 GB or enterprise ECC/support is required. Cloud benchmark candidates: one H200 and one B200 run after the optimized NTT and base-conversion kernels exist. A100/H100 are useful baselines but should not be assumed optimal for integer-heavy FHE. Do not commit to a data-center platform until the same binaries, parameter set, and timing boundaries have been compared. Mandatory cross-GPU benchmark gate ¶ Run the same commit, CUDA version where possible, and fixed clocks/power policy. Record both median and p95 over enough iterations to remove startup effects. Arithmetic microbenchmarks ¶ u32 add/subtract and mul.hi / mul.wide ; u64 add/subtract; 64-by-64 low/high product using __umul64hi ; Shoup multiplication for fixed twiddles; Barrett multiplication for variable operands; the current __uint128_t % q reference path; register count, spills, achieved occupancy, and instructions per result. Memory and NTT tests ¶ coalesced copy and strided gather bandwidth; L2-resident and DRAM-resident cases; shared-memory butterfly throughput; NTT forward/inverse for N = 4,096, 8,192, 16,384, 32,768, 65,536 ; active RNS tower counts representative of early and late CKKS levels; kernel-only latency and end-to-end latency separately. Base conversion and Hybrid key switching ¶ Q to QP and QP to Q conversion by level; digit decomposition; evaluation-key multiply-accumulate; relinearization and rotation; one request and increasing batch sizes; peak device memory with all required keys resident; exact equality against the pinned OpenFHE reference at every intermediate boundary. Selection rule ¶ If RTX 5090 fits the complete resident set and is within 15% of the fastest tested card end to end, keep it as the primary platform. If 32 GB is the only blocker, compare RTX PRO 6000 against H200 rental cost and deployment constraints. If H200/B200 gains track memory bandwidth, prioritize memory-layout and batching work before changing the arithmetic design. If gains track modular-multiply throughput, specialize arithmetic and dispatch by compute capability. Publish measured results; do not rank cards using FP8/FP16 Tensor TOPS. Bottom line ¶ Your teammate is correct that much of RTX 5090 marketing emphasizes FP4/FP8/FP16 AI. That does not make the card unsuitable for FHE. RTX 5090 also has a very large general-purpose CUDA engine, a published 104.8 non-Tensor INT32 TOPS peak, high GDDR7 bandwidth, and a large L2 cache. For this project's current development stage, it is the best-balanced target. The caveat is u64 : NVIDIA does not publish enough information to declare any card the winner from specifications. We should choose RTX 5090 now, keep the arithmetic layer portable, and require the benchmark gate before selecting the production GPU.

title: Benchmarks & tuning
summary: Workload matrix, profiling evidence, and per-device kernel selection.
text: GPU NTT benchmark and tuning plan ¶ Primary target: NVIDIA RTX 5090 ( sm_120 ) Cross-architecture control: NVIDIA RTX 4090 ( sm_89 ) Workload target: OpenFHE 1.6.1 CKKS with Hybrid key switching Ring dimensions: 4096 , 8192 , 16384 , 32768 , 65536 Benchmarking and tuning are deliverables of the project. A kernel is not considered complete merely because it is correct or fast for one transform size. Selection must account for the GPU, CKKS parameters, batch shape, and whether the objective is latency or throughput. 1. Implementations to compare ¶ Each implementation must preserve the same transform convention and pass the same exact correctness gates. Current radix-2 two-pass implementation using reference modular arithmetic. Two-pass implementation with Shoup twiddle multiplication and Barrett or Montgomery variable multiplication. Radix-4 register-staged implementation. Radix-8 register-staged implementation with padded shared memory. Coalesced Four-Step/transpose implementation. Fused variants used by base conversion and Hybrid key switching. External libraries such as GPU-NTT and FIDESlib are comparison baselines when their transform semantics, modulus limits, and timing boundaries can be matched. Their numbers must not be compared directly when one result includes transfers or an entire RNS polynomial and the other does not. 2. Workload matrix ¶ The minimum matrix is: Axis Values Ring dimension 2^12 , 2^13 , 2^14 , 2^15 , 2^16 Modulus width OpenFHE-compatible 50, 55, 59/60-bit primes Active RNS towers representative shallow, medium, and deep CKKS levels Polynomial count one component, full ciphertext, key-switch digits Batch size 1 , 2 , 4 , 8 , then L2-capacity-limited sweep Direction forward, inverse, forward–pointwise–inverse Objective single-operation latency and steady-state throughput Transfer policy device-resident, pinned end-to-end, pageable end-to-end GPU RTX 5090 primary; RTX 4090 control The exact tower counts and Hybrid digit counts must come from the pinned OpenFHE parameter sets used by the inference examples, rather than synthetic three-limb inputs alone. 3. GPU and kernel parameters to tune ¶ Tune or record all of the following: threads per block and blocks per transform; values and butterflies per thread; radix and number of stages fused per kernel; tile/split dimensions and transpose shape; register count per thread and register spilling; static/dynamic shared memory per block and bank conflicts; active blocks and warps per SM; warp-shuffle versus shared-memory exchange boundaries; twiddle layout, Shoup table layout, and on-the-fly twiddle generation; lazy-reduction range and reduction frequency; RNS limb, ciphertext, and operation batch layout; CUDA stream count, asynchronous copies, and CUDA Graph replay; scratch-buffer reuse and allocator behavior. Compiler resource reports ( ptxas -v ) and measured Nsight occupancy must both be retained. A lower register count is not automatically better: the decision criterion is end-to-end performance without spills or unacceptable occupancy. 4. Measurements ¶ Timing ¶ CUDA-event kernel-only latency for every kernel and complete transform; transfer-inclusive latency, separating pinned and pageable host memory; transforms per second and coefficients/towers processed per second; full polynomial multiplication latency; Hybrid key switch, relinearization, rotation, and hoisted-rotation latency; complete encrypted-inference latency and peak device memory; cold setup, warm steady state, and CUDA Graph replay separately. Report median, p5, and p95 after warm-up. Store raw samples so later summaries can be regenerated without rerunning the GPU. Hardware counters ¶ achieved DRAM and L2 bandwidth; global load/store transaction efficiency; L2 hit rate and read/write sectors; shared-memory bank conflicts; registers per thread, spills, occupancy, and eligible warps; SM and memory-pipeline utilization; kernel-launch count and synchronization gaps. The current column pass must specifically record memory sectors per requested byte because its neighboring-thread coefficient addresses are 2,048 bytes apart. 5. Reproducibility record ¶ Every result row must include: GPU name, compute capability, clocks, power mode, and memory size; driver, CUDA toolkit/runtime, compiler, CMake flags, and git commit; implementation/variant ID and all tuned launch parameters; N , modulus bits, actual moduli or parameter-set ID, tower count, digit count, batch shape, transform ordering, and transfer policy; correctness-gate result and profiler command/version; whether setup, allocation, transfers, and synchronization are included. Results without this header are exploratory and must not appear in published comparison tables. 6. Tuning procedure ¶ Run exact arithmetic and transform gates for the candidate variant. Reject variants that spill unexpectedly, exceed resource limits, or violate lazy-reduction bounds. Sweep launch and staging parameters for each supported ring dimension. Profile the best latency and throughput candidates with Nsight Compute. Repeat using realistic RNS tower and Hybrid digit batches. Validate finalists on RTX 4090 to identify architecture-specific choices. Record the winner in a dispatch table keyed by GPU capability, ring dimension, tower/batch range, and latency/throughput mode. Re-run the complete Hybrid key-switch and inference benchmarks. A locally faster NTT variant is accepted only if it improves the target pipeline or supplies a clearly justified fallback. 7. Acceptance gates ¶ Exact forward/inverse agreement for every supported N and OpenFHE modulus. No silent fallback to device-side integer remainder in optimized kernels. No benchmark mixes kernel-only and end-to-end timing boundaries. A selected implementation exists for all five ring dimensions on RTX 5090. RTX 4090 results either validate the same dispatch or document a separate one. Full Hybrid key-switch and inference results accompany NTT microbenchmarks. The HTML explainer identifies which schedule is the correctness baseline and which implementation the tuner selected for each workload class.
